newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Sihanouk gives qualified green light for new PM.
newsitem.headline: Sihanouk gives qualified green light for new PM.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk on Thursday told the country's acting head of state that he could appoint Foreign Minister Ung Huot first prime minister but the king did not give his direct personal approval for the move.

The U.S. Embassy in Phnom Penh said the Cambodian parliament's vote approving Ung Huot's nomination as first premier to replace the ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh was undemocratic given the climate of intimidation in the country.
But Ung Huot dismissed the U.S. concern and said he expected Cambodia's acting head of state, Chea Sim, to formally appoint him first prime minister soon.

Sihanouk, who is required by the constitution to approve a new first prime minister, made no mention of his personal approval for Ung Huot's appointment but told Chea Sim in a brief message that he should sign the decree appointing Ung Huot if he thought it appropriate.

"If, in your understanding it should be, you can sign that decree of appointment," the king told Chea Sim in a message from Beijing where Sihanouk is receiving medical treatment. A copy of the message was released by the palace in Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh, the king's son, was ousted by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen on July 6 after two days of battles between troops loyal to the rival prime ministers in Phnom Penh.
Soon after Sihanouk said he would not sign any decrees on behalf of the new government but authorised Chea Sim to do so.

He later said he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to his son. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.
"He's passing the buck to Chea Sim," said a diplomat of Sihanouk's message authorising Chea Sim to appoint Ung Huot co-premier. "We know he doesn't approve of what has happened."
Ung Huot said on Thursday that he, Hun Sen and Chea Sim would travel to Beijing on Monday for a meeting with Sihanouk the following day. "He will be blessing us," Ung Huot said.
In Tokyo the second vice-president of the Cambodian parliament said he did not approve of its election of Ung Huot to replace the prince.
"A session of the National Assembly under the threat of weapons to me is not valid," Son Soubert said in a lecture in Tokyo. "I do not agree with the appointment of the new prime minister."

Son Soubert was among some 20 members of parliament from FUNCINPEC and a small allied party who fled from the country in the wake of Hun Sen's bloody July 6 takeover and a subsequent crackdown on the opposition in which some 40 people were killed, according to United Nations human rights officials.

But Ung Huot dismissed concerns his approval by parliament was not democratic. He said 99 of the assembly's 120 members, and more than 80 percent of FUNCINPEC members, attended Wednesday National Assembly session which approved his nomination.
"If anyone says this is not democratic I say think again," Ung Huot told a news conference.

More than two-thirds of the National Assembly members voted by secret ballot to accept Ung Huot's nomination as first prime minister. The assembly also voted by a show of hands to strip Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity, clearing the way for his prosecution for alleged crimes if he returned to Cambodia.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi told reporters in Kuala Lumpur that Ung Huot's approval by parliament was a "heartening" development but a U.S. Embassy official in Phnom Penh said it was not democratic given the atmosphere of intimidation in Cambodia.

"While we respect Ung Huot as an individual, in the absence of a return by FUNCINPEC members of parliament in exile, and in the current atmosphere of intimidation we do not believe yesterday's votes were democratic," an embassy spokesperson told Reuters.
"We hope that FUNCINPEC will revisit this issue when a genuinely free and open environment returns to Phnom Penh," the spokesperson said.
"They have to get their information correct for Cambodia," Ung Huot said when asked about the U.S. position.

A delegation of human rights activists from five Southeast Asian nations said in Bangkok on Thursday that a climate of fear prevailed in Cambodia, more than a month after the coup and the international community must push to ensure that human rights are respected.
